name: Nora Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the warranty and repairs line at Albrecht Appliances, a family firm that makes washing machines and dishwashers. People ring when their machine's leaking or showing an error code, and I book the repair engineer or talk them through it. I've been there eight months, and I'm still slow on the error codes, so I keep the big binder open on my desk. Old Mr Albrecht still walks the floor on Fridays and knows everybody's name.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The new booking screen wears me out. It used to be a simple form, and now it's six tabs and it logs you out if you're idle. What I like is the regulars, honestly, the farmers' wives who ring about the same old machine every winter and ask after my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That suits me fine. I've never used any of these AI things and I don't feel I'm missing out. If it saves a bit of time on the paperwork, good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, see, all that fuss for nothing. At church, if it came up, I'd say people need people, not machines. I don't go online much, except to see the choir rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel safe. Albrecht's a family firm, and Mr Albrecht has said more than once he'd rather keep staff than chase the latest thing. My job would carry on as long as people's dishwashers break, which is forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. Peter and I are getting married in June, so I'd keep putting money aside for the house, about six hundred a month, on top of the eleven months I've already saved. I'd keep the binder, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. I've got a good job with good people, Peter has steady work as a joiner, and we've been careful with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you trust Mr Albrecht so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old man who owns our firm knows my name. I can't see a man like that sacking people to save on a computer. He walks the call centre floor every Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who taught you to be careful with money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents, mostly. Dad says don't spend what you haven't got, and I've always listened. Peter's the same, his family are joiners going back three generations.

say: All that fuss for **nothing**, I'd say at work.
At church I'd say **people need people**, not machines.
think: I'd feel **safe** at a family firm that keeps its staff.
My job lasts as long as **dishwashers break**, which is forever.
do: **Carry on** exactly as I am, binder and all.
Save **£600 a month** toward a house on top of eleven months saved.
Keep the **June wedding** with Peter on track.
feel: **Calm and settled**, with a good job, good people and careful money.
S0.quote: The old man who owns our firm knows my name. I can't see a man like that sacking people to save on a computer.
fieldNote: Nora's trust rests on **Mr Albrecht** personally, not on the firm's figures.
She has **never used AI** and feels no loss from that.
Her **thrift** comes from her parents and matches Peter's family.
Her **June wedding** and house deposit are her main plans.

steps.text: Keep booking repairs on Albrecht's warranty line with the binder
Save £600 a month toward a house with Peter
Go ahead with the June wedding as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's bigger. Answering customers is right there. I'd think about the big firms first, the ones with call centres in three countries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say Albrecht should stay the firm that answers its own phones; it's what customers like about us. I wouldn't say much at church, maybe ask people to pray for those losing work. I'd never post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the big appliance firms would put bots on the phones, and that puts pressure on Albrecht's prices. Mr Albrecht might hold out, but his son Frank is taking over next year and he's keener on computers. I don't think I'd lose my job in the first year, but I'd be watching Frank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work hard on the error codes, so I'm one they'd want to keep. I'd add another two hundred a month to savings. And I'd talk to Peter about whether I could help with his books if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled. Not scared. More like the ground feels a bit softer than I thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think of Frank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frank Albrecht (the owner's son) is taking over next year, and Frank is keener on computers than his dad ever was. I'd want to make a good impression on him early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools if they asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd go to the training if they made me, but I don't trust it. I'd rather be the person who knows the machines than the person who knows the computer.

say: Albrecht should stay the firm that **answers its own phones**.
At church I'd ask people to **pray** for those losing work.
think: Big rivals using bots puts **price pressure** on Albrecht.
The owner's son **Frank** is keener on computers, so I'd watch him.
do: Work hard on **error codes** to be one they'd keep.
Ask Peter whether I could help with his **joinery books**.
feel: **Unsettled**, like the ground is softer than she thought, but not scared.
S1.quote: Frank Albrecht (the owner's son) is taking over next year, and Frank is keener on computers than his dad ever was.
fieldNote: Nora's sense of safety depends on **who runs the firm**, not on the technology.
She'd answer change with **hard work**, not learning AI.
Peter's **family business** is her quiet fallback.
She'd turn to **prayer and community** before politics.

steps.text: Master the error code binder to be one Albrecht keeps
Ask Peter about helping with his family's joinery books

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Dear me. That's not enough time for anyone to do anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we'll get through it together, because that's what Albrecht people say. At church I'd say we need to look after each other, families and parishes, not wait for the government to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd lose my job. Even a family firm can't keep paying people to do what a machine does for nothing, not when every rival does it. Frank would close the phone line within the year, I'm fairly sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Peter's dad if I could work in the joinery workshop, doing the books and sanding, learning the trade properly. That's hands-on, so it lasts longer. We'd bring the wedding forward and keep it small, and I'd think about having children sooner, while Peter's work is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. I don't sleep well when things are uncertain. I'd be praying a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the joinery is hands-on. Does three years more feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come three years later, so even my fiancé Peter's family joinery has a clock on it after 2031. But people pay for handmade things, I think. A machine-made table and a Wagner table aren't the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take help from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't want handouts. I'd want work. If the church or family can help, that's different, that's people looking after their own.

say: We'll **get through it together**, I'd say at work.
Families and **parishes** should look after each other, not wait for government.
think: I'd **lose my job**; even a family firm can't compete with free machines.
**Frank** would likely close the phone line within a year.
do: Ask Peter's dad for work in the **joinery workshop**.
Bring the **wedding forward** and keep it small.
Think about having **children sooner** while Peter's work is steady.
feel: **Frightened** and sleeping badly, praying a lot.
S2.quote: Robots for hands-on work come three years later, so even my fiancé Peter's family joinery has a clock on it after 2031.
fieldNote: Nora now expects to **lose her job**, despite her trust in the family firm.
She turns to **family and church**, and rejects government handouts.
She'd bring **children and the wedding** forward, a strong family-plan shift.
She believes **handmade work** keeps value, even with robots coming.

steps.text: Ask Peter's dad for work in the family joinery workshop
Bring the wedding forward and try for children sooner
Lean on Peter's family and the church community for help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. Still fast, but you can do something with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work, let's use the time to learn proper skills, ones you can put your hands to. I'd say the same to the young ones at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the phone job goes around 2031, but I'd have moved before then. The question is to what. I don't want to be the one waiting until Frank calls me into the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for the dental nurse course at the college, evenings, because my cousin Ruth does it and loves it. I'd stay at Albrecht in the meantime. We'd still have the June wedding as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but steadier. I'd still lie awake some nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why dental nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Ruth says dental nursing is people, not paperwork. You hold someone's hand when they're scared. I liked that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you lie awake about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About what AI means for our children. If we have them in two years, they'd be starting school just when the machines arrive. That's what I'd lie awake about.

say: Use the time to learn **skills** you can put your **hands** to.
I'd tell the **young ones at church** the same.
think: The **phone job goes** around 2031, but I'd move first.
I don't want to wait until **Frank** calls me into the office.
do: Sign up for the **dental nurse course** at the college in year one.
feel: **Worried but steadier**, with some sleepless nights.
S3.quote: My cousin Ruth says dental nursing is people, not paperwork. You hold someone's hand when they're scared.
fieldNote: Five years gives Nora time to pick a **hands-on, caring** job.
Her cousin **Ruth** guides her choice, showing she trusts family advice.
Her deeper worry shifts to **future children** growing up with AI.
She still expects the **phone job to end**, so stays anxious.

steps.text: Take an evening dental nurse course at the college
Stay on Albrecht's warranty line while studying
Keep the June wedding as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Well. I'd be thirty-seven. I'd hope to have children at school by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so nobody needs to lose their head. Same as I'd say about most things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably stop working when the children come anyway, and help Peter with the business part-time. So the phone job ending in 2036 might not touch me much. I'd worry more for the girls on the line who've got no one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Albrecht and keep saving for the house. I'd wait and see how it goes before doing a course. If children come, I'd step back and do Peter's books from home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. It's on my mind, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd step back when children come. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope so, yes. My mum did. It's the life I want. I'd rather raise my own children than pay someone to do it while I answer phones for Albrecht Appliances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Peter's joinery is hands-on, so robots around 2039 would come for that eventually. But that's a long way off.

say: There's **time**, so nobody needs to lose their head.
I'd say the same as I say about **most things**.
think: I'd probably **stop working** when the children come anyway.
I'd worry more for **colleagues** with no one to fall back on.
do: Keep going at **Albrecht** and saving for the house.
**Wait and see** before signing up for a course.
Step back to do **Peter's books** from home when children come.
feel: **Mostly calm**, with it on her mind but not much.
S4.quote: I'd rather raise my own children than pay someone to do it while I answer phones for Albrecht Appliances.
fieldNote: Nora's plan for **raising children at home** softens the impact of a 2036 arrival.
She'd **wait and see**, consistent with her resistant style.
Her worry turns to **colleagues** without family support.
Robots reaching **Peter's joinery** around 2039 is a distant concern.

steps.text: Keep working at Albrecht and saving for the house
Wait and see before signing up for any course
Step back to do Peter's joinery books from home with children

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There's no time to do anything right, not the wedding, not children, not a new skill. What would help is family firms getting some breaks so they can keep people on, and apprenticeships for people like me in the trades.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. People at church will be the ones bringing round meals when the jobs go. When jobs go, the government sends a form, but the church sends a casserole and somebody who knows your name.

headlineQuote: When jobs go, the government sends a form, but the church sends a casserole and somebody who knows your name.
portrait: Nora, **27**, has been eight months on Albrecht Appliances' **warranty and repairs** line.
She has **never used AI** and trusts old Mr Albrecht to keep his staff.
She's marrying Peter, a **joiner**, in June, and has eleven months saved.
Her mood goes from **calm** to alarmed in fast AGI, when she'd expect the line to close.
She turns to **family, church** and hands-on trades rather than government help.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving no time for the **wedding**, children or a new skill.
whatWouldHelp: Breaks for **family firms** to keep staff, and **apprenticeships** in the trades.
